promptText: Why do production chat systems default to WebSockets over long polling or Server-Sent Events for the core messaging transport?
options: A WebSocket upgrades a single TCP connection into a persistent, full-duplex channel, letting both sides push at any time with low per-message overhead, which matches chat's genuinely bidirectional traffic pattern
Long polling and SSE cannot be served over standard HTTP infrastructure, while WebSockets can
WebSockets are the only transport capable of being encrypted with TLS
SSE already supports full bidirectional communication, so WebSockets only add redundant overhead on top of it
explanation: Chat requires both sending and receiving over the same session, and a WebSocket provides that over one persistent, full-duplex connection with low per-message overhead, which compounds once a session exchanges thousands of small messages. SSE is explicitly one-directional (server-to-client only), so it still needs an ordinary request for the client to send, making it a half-duplex fit for a full-duplex problem; long polling works over plain HTTP but re-pays a full request/response cycle per cycle.

promptText: Why is conversation_id the correct partition key for the message store, rather than user_id?
options: The dominant read pattern is "recent messages for this one conversation," so partitioning by conversation_id keeps that query within a single shard, while partitioning by user_id would scatter one conversation's messages across every participant's shard
user_id partitioning is impossible because user IDs are not guaranteed unique across shards
conversation_id partitioning removes the need for any composite sort key within a partition
user_id partitioning guarantees perfectly even load across shards regardless of access pattern, which conversation_id cannot match
explanation: Almost every chat read is "give me this conversation's recent messages," never "every message this user ever sent across all conversations," so partitioning by conversation_id lets that common query touch exactly one shard. Partitioning by user_id instead would require fetching and merging fragments of the same conversation from multiple shards for every participant, which is exactly the mistake the chapter calls out.

promptText: Why does a conversation-scoped, monotonically increasing sequence number beat a wall-clock timestamp as the ordering key for messages in a conversation?
options: Clock skew between servers (or between client and server clocks) can make timestamps of messages sent moments apart compare in the wrong order, or tie outright, while a sequence number from a single authoritative assignment point gives a strict, gap-free order regardless of clock behavior
Timestamps consume more storage per row than an integer sequence number, which is the primary reason to avoid them
Sequence numbers let the system automatically expire and delete old messages once a threshold is reached
Sequence numbers encode which specific sender produced each message, which timestamps cannot represent
explanation: A timestamp depends on clocks that can skew between machines, so two messages sent close together can tie or even appear reversed; a sequence number assigned by one authoritative point per conversation sidesteps clock behavior entirely and guarantees a strict total order, which is why it is treated as the real fix rather than timestamp precision or storage size.

promptText: Why must a message be durably persisted and sequenced before any delivery attempt is made, rather than attempting delivery first?
options: If delivery were attempted before persistence, a crash or failure during that delivery attempt could leave the message lost entirely with nothing durable to retry against, whereas a persisted message can always have delivery retried later
WebSocket connections require the server to hold a database lock before any frame can be sent
Persisting first allows the system to skip assigning a sequence number altogether
Attempting delivery first would violate the at-least-once delivery guarantee used by the push notification provider
explanation: Persisting the message first means durability never depends on whether the recipient happens to be reachable at that instant; if a failure occurs during a delivery attempt afterward, the message still exists durably and delivery can simply be retried, whereas attempting delivery first risks losing the message outright if something fails before it is ever written down.

promptText: Why are media attachments (images, video, files) stored in dedicated object storage and only referenced by ID from the message row, rather than embedded inline?
options: Embedding media inline would make the message store's size and replication cost dominated by attachment size rather than by actual message volume, the wrong thing to optimize a high-write-rate message table for
Relational and wide-column databases are physically incapable of storing any binary data in a row
Object storage is the only system capable of generating a secure, time-limited download URL
Storing media inline would make it impossible to assign a sequence number to the message
explanation: The chapter's storage-growth math shows message metadata alone is already substantial at scale; embedding media bytes inline would make the message store's size and replication cost dominated by attachment size instead of message volume, which is why message bodies are kept separate from media stored in object storage and referenced only by ID or URL.

promptText: Why is presence ("online," "last seen 5 minutes ago") implemented as a TTL-based entry in a fast store refreshed by heartbeats, rather than a row updated in a durable database on every heartbeat?
options: Writing a durable, typically indexed database row on every heartbeat from every connected user would itself be a severe write-amplification problem, and presence doesn't need the strong durability a message does, so a TTL-based entry with a short expiry is the standard, cheaper approach
A durable per-heartbeat database row is actually the cheaper option at scale, but TTL entries are used anyway for historical compatibility with IRC
TTL-based entries guarantee presence is always accurate to the millisecond, unlike a database row
WebSocket connections are incapable of sending periodic heartbeat signals, so TTL expiry is the only viable detection mechanism
explanation: Presence is inherently a best-effort, eventually-consistent inference rather than a strongly guaranteed fact, so writing a durable row on every heartbeat from every connected user would be an enormous, unnecessary write-amplification cost; a TTL-based record in a fast in-memory store (expiring if no heartbeat refreshes it in time) achieves the same practical outcome far more cheaply.

promptText: Why can't a standard load balancer simply route "deliver this message to user X" the way it routes an ordinary HTTP request to any healthy backend?
options: Once a gateway server accepts a client's WebSocket connection, that instance becomes the one specific machine physically holding that socket, so delivery requires a connection-registry lookup to find and reach that exact instance, not any interchangeable healthy one
Load balancers are only capable of round-robin routing and cannot be configured with any other algorithm for WebSocket traffic
The message service never knows the recipient's user ID until after the load balancer has already routed the request
WebSocket connections are stateless in the same way HTTP requests are, so any gateway instance could serve them interchangeably
explanation: A load balancer's usual assumption is that any healthy backend can serve a given request because no backend holds caller-specific state; a chat gateway breaks that assumption the moment it accepts a WebSocket, since only that specific instance holds the live socket. The connection registry exists precisely to answer "which exact instance holds this user's connection right now" so the message can be routed there specifically.

promptText: Why does fan-out-on-write work as the uncontested default for chat groups, while a social media feed needs a hybrid fan-out strategy for its largest producers?
options: Chat group sizes are bounded, typically to a few hundred members, so immediate delivery to every member is cheap and uniform; a feed producer can have millions of followers, making uniform fan-out-on-write prohibitively expensive specifically for the highest-follower accounts
Chat messages are always smaller in byte size than feed posts, which is what makes fan-out-on-write affordable
Fan-out-on-read is technically impossible to implement for a chat conversation due to how sequence numbers are assigned
Chat systems actually use fan-out-on-read by default, while feed systems use fan-out-on-write by default
explanation: Fan-out-on-write's cost scales directly with recipient count; a chat group capped at a few hundred members makes that cost trivial and uniform, whereas a feed producer with millions of followers turns the same strategy into a hot-key problem for just the highest-follower accounts, forcing a hybrid approach that chat's architecturally smaller scale ceiling never needs to adopt.

promptText: Why should a push notification sent to an offline recipient's device carry only a lightweight "you have a new message" signal instead of the full message content?
options: Push notifications are delivered through a third-party provider (APNs/FCM) outside the application's own trust boundary, so a thin payload limits exposure and lets the client fetch authoritative, current content over its own authenticated channel once it wakes up
Push notification providers charge significantly more per byte for larger payloads, making thin payloads purely a cost optimization
Push notification payloads are structurally incapable of carrying more than a boolean flag
Full message content would make it impossible for the client to later request a catch-up using its last-known sequence number
explanation: A push provider is a third party outside the system's own trust boundary, so sending full content through it unnecessarily widens the data's exposure surface — especially relevant for an end-to-end encrypted product where the server may not even be able to produce readable content. A thin alert that triggers the client to fetch real content over its own authenticated channel keeps the trust boundary where it belongs.

promptText: Why does Spring's built-in simple in-memory STOMP message broker fail to deliver messages correctly in a multi-instance production deployment?
options: The in-memory broker only knows about WebSocket sessions connected to that specific JVM instance, so a message handled by Instance A never reaches a recipient whose socket is held by Instance B
STOMP as a protocol does not support sending messages to more than one recipient at a time
Spring WebSocket endpoints cannot be placed behind a load balancer at all, regardless of broker configuration
The in-memory broker encrypts every message with an instance-specific key that other instances cannot decode
explanation: The simple broker's session knowledge is scoped to the single JVM it runs in, so it has no way to forward a message to a socket held by a different instance; production deployments replace it with an external relay (a real broker, or Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka) so delivery doesn't silently depend on sender and recipient sharing the same server.

promptText: A user is logged into the same chat account on both a phone and a laptop simultaneously. What must the connection registry support that a single-device design would not need?
options: It must map a user to a set of active gateway connections rather than a single one, since the same user can hold live sockets on different gateway instances at once, and a message must fan out to every entry in that set
It must pick whichever device connected most recently and silently drop the connection registry entry for the other device
It must require both devices to share a single WebSocket connection routed through one gateway instance
It must rely entirely on push notifications instead of live delivery whenever more than one device is connected
explanation: Multi-device support means a single user can have multiple simultaneous live connections, possibly to different gateway instances, so the registry must track a set of connections per user rather than one, and delivery and read-status reconciliation must account for every entry in that set rather than assuming a single socket owns the user.

promptText: Why is a wide-column store (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Bigtable) commonly preferred over a relational database for message storage at very high message volume?
options: Its native partition-key-plus-clustering-key model keeps all of one conversation's messages physically co-located and pre-sorted, matching chat's dominant read pattern and append-heavy write pattern more directly than a relational table bolting on a composite index
Relational databases are incapable of defining a composite index on (conversation_id, sequence)
Wide-column stores provide stronger cross-partition ACID transaction guarantees than relational databases, which chat requires
A wide-column store removes the need to choose any partition key at all, since it distributes rows automatically
explanation: A wide-column store's partition-key-plus-clustering-key design natively produces exactly the shape chat needs — one conversation's messages co-located and pre-sorted — and scales the append-mostly, high-volume write pattern more cheaply than a relational database, which can model the same query with a composite index but tends to cost more operationally to scale write throughput at very high volume.

promptText: How should fan-out be adapted for a single very large public channel (100,000+ members) that coexists with normal small group chats, without redesigning the rest of the system?
options: Keep fan-out-on-write as the default for ordinary small conversations, but classify channels above a defined member-count threshold into a separate path that pushes in real time only to currently-connected members and lets less-active members pull on next open, borrowing the feed system's hybrid idea for just that case
Apply fan-out-on-write uniformly to every conversation regardless of member count, since chat's bounded group sizes make the write cost trivial no matter how large a channel grows
Replace WebSockets with plain HTTP polling for every client whenever any single channel in the system exceeds a few hundred members
Re-shard the connection registry by conversation ID so that every member of a large channel connects to the same gateway instance
explanation: At tens or hundreds of thousands of members, uniform fan-out-on-write starts to resemble the social-feed hot-key problem chat normally avoids; the fix is to classify conversations by member count and give only the ones above a threshold a different, read-leaning delivery path for inactive members, rather than paying that extra complexity for every conversation or abandoning the live-push model entirely.

promptText: A chat product adds true end-to-end encryption so the server never sees plaintext message content. What does this force, beyond the key-exchange mechanics themselves?
options: Server-side full-text search and server-generated rich notification previews both become impossible since the server cannot read the content, forcing replacements like client-side search indexes and client-decrypted previews, along with giving up server-side content-based spam/abuse scanning
Nothing changes architecturally beyond encrypting data at rest, since the server can still run full-text search and generate previews from the stored ciphertext directly
It eliminates the need for a connection registry, since encrypted messages no longer require routing to a specific gateway instance
It allows fan-out-on-write to be replaced entirely by fan-out-on-read, since encrypted payloads are cheaper to re-fetch than to push
explanation: Once content is encrypted end-to-end, the server stores and routes only opaque ciphertext, so it can no longer run full-text search over content, generate readable push previews, or apply server-side content-based abuse scanning; a product adopting E2E has to deliberately rebuild these client-side (on-device search index, client-decrypted previews) or accept the permanent loss, a trade-off distinct from the connection-routing or fan-out mechanics.

promptText: The connection/presence registry (Redis) suffers a partial outage. How should the system degrade gracefully rather than fail outright, and what capacity assumption does that fallback break?
options: Treat recipients whose routing can't be resolved as effectively offline and fall back to the store-and-forward/push-notification path, but that path must be provisioned to absorb a sudden surge of effectively all online users, a very different load than the normal small trickle of actually-offline users it was likely sized for
Drop messages that can't be routed during the outage, since there is no safe fallback once the registry is unavailable
Have every gateway instance broadcast every message to all other instances during the outage, which fully replaces the registry's function with no downside
Extend the registry's TTL to never expire so that entries persist correctly through any outage
explanation: Since the registry sits on the hot path for every delivery, the graceful response is to route affected users through the existing store-and-forward and push-notification path rather than dropping messages; the second-order catch is that this fallback path, normally sized for a small fraction of users being offline, must suddenly absorb close to the entire online population at once, a capacity assumption that needs explicit headroom rather than being discovered during the outage.
